summary: Metadoxine (pyridoxine-pyrrolidone carboxylate, also called pyritinol-related metadoxine) is a metabolic agent used to accelerate clearance of ethanol and acetaldehyde. It is used for acute alcohol intoxication and for alcoholic liver disease, and historically as an adjunct in chronic alcoholism, to reduce alcohol-related symptoms and support liver recovery. Typical oral dosing is 500 mg two to three times daily, with parenteral (IV/IM) doses around 300-900 mg used in the acute intoxication setting. It is generally well tolerated; caution is advised in Parkinson disease or with levodopa (potential for reduced levodopa effect via pyridoxine) and in asthmatic patients because some parenteral formulations contain parabens. It is not FDA-approved; this record is sourced from EMA/SmPC, BNF, and clinical literature.

moa: Metadoxine enhances the activity of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase pathways, accelerating the breakdown and urinary elimination of ethanol and its toxic intermediate acetaldehyde. By reducing acetaldehyde accumulation it limits oxidative stress in hepatocytes, helps replenish reduced glutathione and ATP, and counters the fall in liver NAD+/NADH ratio caused by alcohol. The pyridoxine (vitamin B6) and pyrrolidone carboxylate moieties contribute to restoring cellular metabolic balance, supporting liver function and reducing alcohol-related neuro-behavioral symptoms.

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been adequately established; data are limited. Avoid use unless the benefit clearly justifies the risk.
lact: It is not established whether metadoxine or pyridoxine is excreted in human milk in clinically relevant amounts; high-dose pyridoxine may suppress lactation. Use with caution and per clinical judgment.
renal: Limited data on use in renal impairment; metadoxine and metabolites are renally eliminated, so use with caution and consider dose reduction in significant impairment.
hepatic: Indicated in alcoholic liver disease and generally used to support hepatic recovery; follow clinical guidance and monitor liver function during therapy.

moderate: Levodopa - the pyridoxine (vitamin B6) component can reduce levodopa effectiveness (in the absence of a decarboxylase inhibitor); avoid or use with caution in Parkinson disease
minor: Other vitamin B6-containing supplements - additive pyridoxine exposure

missed: If you miss an oral dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses at once. Parenteral dosing for acute intoxication is given under medical supervision.
overdose: Overdose experience is limited; expected effects relate mainly to the pyridoxine component, where excessive or prolonged high intake can cause sensory peripheral neuropathy. Manage with discontinuation and supportive care; provide symptomatic treatment for any hypersensitivity.
